The Pacific tree frog (Pseudacris regilla) deposits its eggs in gelatinous clusters attached to submerged vegetation in ephemeral ponds and slow-moving streams. Each fertilised ovum is initially quite small, reflecting a wet weight at birth of just 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams], a mass derived from the typical egg diameter of approximately 2 millimeters. This modest investment per offspring is common among hylid frogs that produce large clutches. The eggs begin development immediately after ovum activation, and the duration of embryogenesis is strongly temperature-dependent. At a constant incubation temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], a consistent developmental schedule emerges: the first larval eclosion, or hatching event, occurs after roughly 24.5 days [ab = roughly 24.5 days]. This relatively rapid embryonic period at elevated temperatures allows larvae to enter the aquatic environment quickly, taking advantage of warm, productive vernal pools before they begin to dry.

Following eclosion, the newly emerged tadpoles enter a lecithotrophic phase during which they rely entirely on residual yolk reserves for sustenance. This non-feeding stage is brief, as the buccal apparatus develops rapidly and the exotrophic transition—marked by first exogenous feeding—occurs within days. The aquatic larva then enters a prolonged period of rapid growth and filter feeding on algae and detritus. Under laboratory conditions maintained at a steady 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the time since birth at metamorphosis has been measured at approximately 91.5 days since birth . This developmental milestone, during which the larva undergoes the full suite of morphological transformations including limb bud development and tail resorption, is completed when the juvenile froglet emerges onto land. The timing of this metamorphic climax is a critical life history event that determines the quality of the terrestrial recruit entering the population.

After completing metamorphosis, the terrestrial juvenile amphibian—now a fully terrestrial froglet—enters a post-metamorphic growth phase. Young individuals feed on small arthropods and continue to increase in body size. The duration of this juvenile period before the attainment of sexual maturity has been documented in field and captive studies. Measurements taken under thermal conditions typical of the species active season, at a reference temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], indicate that the time since metamorphosis at puberty for females is approximately 547.5 days since metamorphosis [tp = approximately 547.5 days since metamorphosis]. This extended sub-adult period allows females to accumulate substantial somatic resources before initiating reproduction, a strategy that supports the production of large clutch masses in subsequent breeding seasons. The onset of gonadal maturation is accompanied by distinct changes in behaviour and secondary sexual characteristics, including the development of the vocal sac in males.

Adult females of Pseudacris regilla attain a maximum recorded body mass in adults that is considerably larger than that of males, reflecting the substantial energetic investment in egg production. The ultimate wet weight for females reaches approximately 2.76 grams [Wwi = approximately 2.76 grams], a size that correlates strongly with fecundity. During the breeding season, which is triggered by rainfall and warming temperatures, reproductively active adults congregate at breeding ponds. Reproductive output in this species has been quantified in several populations. When maintained at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], female Pacific tree frogs exhibit a maximum reproduction rate that can be expressed as a combination of clutch size and spawning frequency. Individual females produce between 300 and 750 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 300 and 750 eggs per clutch], and they typically deposit about 0.13 clutches per year [F_R_i = about 0.13 clutches per year], a low annual frequency that aligns with their relatively long lifespan and iteroparous breeding strategy.

Maximum lifespan in the wild has been recorded through mark-recapture studies extending over multiple breeding seasons. The oldest documented individual observed under natural conditions lived for approximately 9 years [am = approximately 9 years], a remarkably long lifespan for a small hylid frog of at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]this body size. This longevity is sustained by a low resting metabolic demand; measurements of basal oxygen consumption taken at 20 °C [T = 20 °C] reveal a maximum basal metabolic rate of 0.0027 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 0.0027 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that underscores the species comparatively slow life-history pace. The combination of a modest metabolic rate, a prolonged juvenile period, and a low annual reproductive effort allows individuals to spread their reproductive investment across many breeding seasons, thereby buffering against the high environmental stochasticity typical of temporary wetland habitats.
